compareCandidate.label: Coefficient vs. subscript
compareCandidate.description: A coefficient is the big number in FRONT of a formula — it counts how many whole units. A subscript is the small number INSIDE a formula — it counts atoms within one unit. 2H₂O means two water molecules; the 2 subscript means two hydrogens in each.

parts: A number in front of a formula
Counts whole units of a substance
processes: Multiplying every atom in the formula it fronts
Making the atom count equal on both sides
plainLanguageExplanation: A coefficient is the number written in front of a chemical formula, and it tells you how many of that unit take part in a reaction. Look at 2H₂O. The big 2 in front is the coefficient — it means two whole water molecules. It multiplies everything in the formula: two water molecules means 4 hydrogens total and 2 oxygens. This is different from the small subscript — the 2 in H₂O — which counts atoms INSIDE one molecule. Big number in front counts units; small number inside counts atoms per unit. Coefficients are the heart of balancing equations. Consider the reaction H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. Left side: 2 hydrogens and 2 oxygens. Right side: 2 hydrogens but only 1 oxygen. Unbalanced! We need coefficients: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Now both sides have 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens — balanced. Choosing the right coefficients is balancing — it ensures every atom is conserved and obeys the law of conservation of mass.

whyItMatters: Coefficients turn a chemical sentence into a precise recipe. They are how chemists balance equations, predict exactly how much of each substance reacts and forms, and obey conservation of mass. Without coefficients, chemistry could not count — and counting atoms is what makes chemistry a science.
tagline: The multiplier in front of the formula
didYouKnow: The chemical formulas for cellular respiration are a balancing act: one glucose and six oxygens in, six carbons and six waters out — the coefficients tell the whole story.
compareReason: Coefficients are the tool and a balanced equation is the goal — comparing them shows exactly what balancing an equation accomplishes.
